name: Spiny hill turtle
globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition

profile.summary: A forest-floor turtle with an especially striking shell when young. Singapore's remaining mature forests shelter this locally Endangered reptile.
profile.identification: Brown shell with a raised middle ridge and jagged rear edge; dark head and limbs, with reddish marks beside the head. Young turtles have much sharper shell-edge projections than adults.
profile.diet: An omnivore. Regional research records fruit and other plant material, some animal food and mushrooms; the proportions in Singapore have not been measured here.
profile.activity: NParks describes mainly nocturnal activity; this is not a rule that excludes daytime encounters.
profile.behaviour: Adults spend much of their time on land. Younger turtles use water more extensively, so forest-floor and stream habitats both matter.
profile.reproduction: Lays eggs. Breeding has been achieved in conservation collections; no Singapore nesting month or clutch-size claim is made here.
profile.singapore: Native populations are associated with the Central Nature Reserves. The national assessment is Endangered in RDB3; encounter locations and resting sites are not mapped here.
profile.ecologicalRole: Consumes material from several parts of the forest food web. Mushroom eating is documented, but effective fungal-spore dispersal by this species remains a research question.
profile.pressures: Forest degradation and collection for trade threaten it. Protecting habitat and preventing collection are central conservation needs.
profile.watch: Keep to open paths, leave it where it is and avoid handling or flash. Do not disclose a precise location or collect an animal for a pet.

funFacts.title: Growing out of the spikes
funFacts.text: Its dramatic juvenile shell edges become much less spiky as the turtle grows.

funFacts.title: Mushroom on the menu
funFacts.text: A study published in 2026 describes a wild spiny turtle eating a mushroom in Borneo, an observation made in 2020.

name: Asian leaf turtle
globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition

profile.summary: A secretive stream-associated turtle, listed as Critically Endangered in Singapore. Its subdued colours fit the shaded forest setting.
profile.identification: An oval, dark-brown shell with a toothed rear edge; orange lines mark the dark head and neck. Hatchlings are flatter and more densely spotted than adults.
profile.diet: An omnivore that eats both plant and animal material.
profile.activity: NParks describes apparent nocturnal activity; detailed Singapore activity patterns remain poorly documented.
profile.behaviour: Associated with forest streams and their banks. Limited sightings make this an animal to learn about without seeking out sensitive sites.
profile.reproduction: Lays eggs; local nesting timing and clutch sizes have not been verified.
profile.singapore: NParks documents catchment-forest records from 2006 and 2007. These are historical observations, while RDB3 (2024) retains the species as nationally Critically Endangered; neither is a current population census.
profile.ecologicalRole: Its mixed diet connects plant material and animal prey within the forest-stream food web.
profile.pressures: Habitat degradation and collection for food or trade are identified threats. Forest streams and surrounding cover need protection.
profile.watch: Stay out of streams and leave turtles, eggs and cover undisturbed. Do not collect or release pet turtles into natural habitats.

funFacts.title: Baby shell, different look
funFacts.text: The hatchling has a flattened shell densely patterned with dark spots; adults have a dark-brown shell.

funFacts.title: A hidden splash of colour
funFacts.text: Look at the reference photo: the dark head and neck carry orange lines.

name: Clouded monitor
globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition

profile.summary: A native monitor that is as comfortable climbing trees as exploring the forest floor. It generally favours land habitats more than the familiar water monitor.
profile.identification: Brown with yellow spotting. Compared with a Malayan water monitor, the head is shorter, the tail more rounded and the nostril sits farther back, about midway between the eye and snout tip. Use several features together.
profile.diet: Searches through leaf litter for worms and other invertebrates.
profile.activity: Diurnal: active during daylight, as documented in local forest surveys.
profile.behaviour: Forages on the ground and climbs trees. Its ability to use both levels is a useful reminder to look above ground as well as along paths.
profile.reproduction: Lays eggs. Local nesting dates, clutch size and incubation periods are not asserted from unrelated captive accounts.
profile.singapore: NParks describes it as relatively common in suitable habitats, including forest and wooded gardens. This does not mean it is equally frequent in every neighbourhood.
profile.ecologicalRole: A predator of small ground-dwelling animals within the leaf-litter food web.
profile.pressures: Retaining forest cover, leaf litter and climbing trees helps preserve its habitat. Its local Least Concern label does not remove the need for respectful encounters.
profile.watch: Watch from a distance and allow it to pass. Never feed, corner or handle a monitor, and keep pets under control.

funFacts.title: The nose knows
funFacts.text: Nostril position helps tell the two common monitors apart: the clouded monitor's nostril sits farther back from the snout tip.

funFacts.title: A lizard upstairs
funFacts.text: Clouded monitors forage on land but can also climb trees.

name: Malayan horned frog
globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition

profile.summary: A leaf-shaped ambush hunter from Singapore's mature forests. Its camouflage is so effective that a call may reveal a frog that the eye has missed.
profile.identification: Broad angular head, pointed eyelid projections and a leaf-like snout and brown body. Females are larger than males. Projection length varies, so it should not be the only identification feature.
profile.diet: Animal prey on the forest floor, including invertebrates and small vertebrates such as other frogs or lizards.
profile.activity: Secretive; calls can be heard around dusk and were recorded during late-afternoon breeding observations in Singapore.
profile.behaviour: Remains still in leaf litter and ambushes passing prey. Local researchers have often detected it by its distinctive loud call near streams.
profile.reproduction: Breeds in forest streams. A Singapore field study recorded mating and a cluster of gelatinous eggs attached beneath partly submerged bark; larvae develop in water.
profile.singapore: Associated with patches of mature forest in the Central Nature Reserves. It is nationally Critically Endangered in RDB3; this guide avoids breeding-site directions.
profile.ecologicalRole: An ambush predator that connects leaf-litter prey with larger forest predators; its aquatic young also depend on stream habitat.
profile.pressures: Loss or damage to moist forest and stream habitat is a concern, alongside collection for the pet trade across its range.
profile.watch: Listen from open trails during permitted hours. Do not use call playback, move leaf litter, enter breeding streams or handle frogs and eggs.

funFacts.title: A leaf with legs
funFacts.text: Its angular outline and brown colouring help a motionless frog disappear among fallen leaves.

funFacts.title: Tadpole with a funnel
funFacts.text: The tadpole's broad funnel-shaped mouth helps it feed at the water surface.

name: Black-eyed litter frog
rarity: Elusive; common within some forest habitat
globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition

profile.summary: A small leaf-litter frog with conspicuous dark eyes and a surprisingly distinctive voice. Being common within a forest patch does not mean it is widespread across Singapore.
profile.identification: Large head and black eyes, relatively short slender limbs, and grey or brown skin marked with irregular dark patches. The pale underside has dark speckling.
profile.diet: Insectivorous, feeding on small animal prey in its forest-floor habitat.
profile.behaviour: Lives among fallen leaves. Its rapid rattling call can be easier to notice than its camouflaged body.
profile.reproduction: Has an aquatic tadpole stage. NParks describes the larvae as large and almost black; no verified Singapore clutch-size or fixed breeding-season estimate is supplied here.
profile.singapore: Associated with the Central Nature Reserves and forest stream habitats. NParks surveys found it frequently in suitable forest, while RDB3 assesses it as nationally Near Threatened.
profile.ecologicalRole: An insect predator within the forest-floor food web, with aquatic larvae linking the life cycle to water.
profile.pressures: Maintaining connected, moist forest and its water habitats is important for this habitat-associated frog; local frequency should not be confused with habitat security.
profile.watch: Observe without moving logs or leaves. Keep out of streams, avoid playback and flash, and leave amphibians and tadpoles untouched.

funFacts.title: Tiny frog, rapid rattle
funFacts.text: Researchers identify its rapid, rattling call even when the frog itself stays hidden.

funFacts.title: A frog doing a handstand
funFacts.text: A Singapore observation documented one balancing on its front limbs while wiping its body with its back feet; the purpose was not proven.
